outcome: Nothing has settled whether every Fermat number F_n = 2^(2^n)+1 with n > 4 is composite, and no Fermat prime beyond F_4 is known; since 26 January 2024 the bearing events are seven new explicit prime factors of individual Fermat numbers (May 2024 to December 2025), each adding one composite index and none moving the universal claim, plus a self-published July 2026 Lean and measurement note on F_5 to F_11 that names Claude and an internal research system as co-authors but does not bear on compositeness for n > 4.
problem_asks: One universal claim, with no separate parts: that F_n = 2^(2^n)+1 is composite for every integer n > 4 (equivalently, that no F_n with n >= 5 is prime). The Wikipedia January 2024 bullet reads 'Is every Fermat number 2^(2^n)+1 composite for n > 4?' and links to the Fermat number article. The question is about the whole family; it does not ask for the factorisation of any particular F_n. Separate questions in the same article, not asked here: whether there are infinitely many Fermat primes, whether there are infinitely many composite Fermat numbers, and whether any Fermat number is not square-free (the last is a separate Wikipedia bullet).

events.what_happened: Euler showed F_5 = 2^32 + 1 = 641 x 6700417, the first Fermat number shown composite, refuting Fermat's expectation that every F_n is prime. The Wikipedia Fermat number article (opened) gives the factorisation and the year 1732; I did not open a primary source.
events.delivers: A single explicit instance: F_5 is composite. It is the n = 5 case of the claim and nothing beyond it.
events.remains: The universal claim for all n > 4, and every n >= 6 individually.
events.object: The explicit factorisation F_5 = 641 x 6700417, both factors explicit.

events.what_happened: Crandall, Mayer and Papadopoulos show F_24 = 2^(2^24)+1 (5,050,446 decimal digits) composite. The method is a rigorous Pepin test, run by two independently written floating-point programs on two physically separate processors whose final residues agree; a separate integer-only algorithm was also used to check the chain. No proper factor was found, and the final residue was deposited in case a factor is later found. Published as 'The twenty-fourth Fermat number is composite', Math. Comp. 72 (2003), 1555-1572. The AMS page returned HTTP 403 and the Reed College PDF could not be decoded, so these details come from search-result summaries.
events.revisions: Preprint dated 28 Jan 2001 on the Reed College site, per the search-result summary (not confirmed on the page). Prime Pages credits a 1999 proof, which reads as the computation date rather than a written argument. Journal publication 2003. The first public written argument is taken to be the 2001 preprint; this date is the least certain in the record.
events.delivers: Compositeness of F_24, with no explicit factor. Settles the n = 24 case only. Per the Crandall note summarised in search results, the open cases among 5 <= n <= 32 in the early 1980s were n = 20, 22, 24, 28 and 31; this event closes one of them.
events.remains: Every other n > 4, including n = 20 (composite, but no known factor) and every n >= 33, and the universal claim itself.

checked_by.who: Referees and editors of Mathematics of Computation (AMS)
checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted the paper for publication. Inferred from the publication record only; the AMS page returned 403 and was not read.

machine_checked.system: Two independently written Pepin-test programs (floating-point DWT) on two machines, plus an integer-only check; a computer calculation, not a proof assistant

events.directly_checkable: Repeat the Pepin test for F_24 from the deposited residue or from scratch; a multi-million-digit computation. Not run.
events.object: No factor is given. The result is that the Pepin residue for F_24 is not the value a prime would give, so F_24 is composite. It is non-constructive about any factor, and the residue was deposited.

events.what_happened: Kent D. Boklan and John H. Conway, 'Expect at most one billionth of a new Fermat Prime!', arXiv:1605.01371, first posted 4 May 2016 (abstract opened: 'We provide compelling evidence that all Fermat primes were already known to Fermat.'). The argument is heuristic: it treats F_n as prime with probability roughly that of a random integer of its size, sums over n >= 33, and bounds the expected number of further Fermat primes at about 2^-30. The search summary also reports an extended version of a paper in The Mathematical Intelligencer; that was not opened.
events.revisions: A v2 is listed on arXiv (seen in search results; not read). The Intelligencer version is not dated here.
events.delivers: Not a result about compositeness. It is a heuristic argument that a Fermat prime beyond F_4 is very unlikely, which points at the composite answer for n > 4 without establishing it. Its own authors frame the estimate as conditional and invite a counter-argument.
events.remains: The whole claim. The heuristic gives an upper bound on the expected number of exceptions, not a proof that there are none.
events.directly_checkable: The estimate is a short calculation from the stated probability model. The model is the point of contention, not the arithmetic.
events.doubts: The estimate assumes Fermat numbers behave like random integers of their size. The Wikipedia Fermat number article (opened) describes the heuristic as not a rigorous proof and notes that Fermat numbers have special divisibility properties that the model ignores.
events.direction: Heuristically toward composite for n > 4 (no further Fermat primes expected). Not a proof either way.

events.what_happened: FermatSearch's news log records a factor 7 x 2^(18233956)+1 of F_18233954, reported 5 October 2020 by Ryan Propper, bringing the count to 354 known Fermat factors. The Wikipedia article (opened, Dec 2025 snapshot) gives the same factor and calls F_18233954 the largest Fermat number known to be composite.
events.delivers: One more composite index with an explicit prime factor. It is the largest index currently known composite, which does not touch the universal claim beyond that one index.
events.remains: Every n > 4 except 18233954, and the universal claim itself.
events.directly_checkable: 7 x 2^(18233956)+1 divides F_18233954 iff 2^(2^18233954) = -1 mod that prime, which needs 18233954 modular squarings. Heavy; not run.
events.object: The explicit prime factor 7 x 2^(18233956)+1 of F_18233954, as printed on FermatSearch and in the Wikipedia article.

events.what_happened: Savino Detto, 'The new Fermat-type factorization algorithm', arXiv:2503.07151, submitted 10 March 2025 (v4 dated 22 September 2026). It is a method for factoring odd integers that halves the iterations of Fermat's factorisation algorithm (FFA-1). The abstract opened does not mention Fermat numbers of the form 2^(2^n)+1.
events.revisions: v1 10 Mar 2025; v4 22 Sep 2026 (per the arXiv abstract page). Only the abstract was read.
events.delivers: Nothing on Fermat numbers. It is a general integer-factoring improvement, a different question from whether F_n is composite.
events.direction: Not applicable: it does not address the composite question.

events.what_happened: FermatSearch news (opened): Gary Gostin reports the factor 322,072,887,044,529 x 2^253+1 of F_251, dated 24 May 2024, found with gfs on an Intel i9-9900K and RTX 4070, and states the total at 369 known Fermat factors. The Riesel Prime divisor page for the same factor, dated 2024-05-24, was seen in search results and not opened.
events.delivers: F_251 has a proper factor, so F_251 is composite. One more index with an explicit factor. The universal claim for n > 4 is not moved beyond this index.
events.remains: The universal claim for all n > 4, and every other index.
events.directly_checkable: Test whether 2^(2^251) = -1 mod 322072887044529 x 2^253+1: 251 modular squarings modulo a 90-bit prime. Cheap. Not run (see incomplete).
events.object: Explicit proper factor 322,072,887,044,529 x 2^253+1 of F_251, as printed.

events.what_happened: FermatSearch news (opened): Serge Batalov and Ryan Propper, with FermatSearch, report the factor 56,073 x 2^223,382+1 of F_223,380, dated 4 July 2024; the page states the total at 370 known Fermat factors.
events.delivers: F_223380 has a proper factor, so it is composite. One more explicit index. Does not move the universal claim beyond this index.
events.remains: The universal claim for all n > 4, and every other index.
events.directly_checkable: 2^(2^223380) = -1 mod p for p of about 223,000 bits: about 223,000 modular squarings at that size. Heavy; not run.
events.object: Explicit proper factor 56,073 x 2^223,382+1 of F_223,380, as printed.

events.what_happened: FermatSearch news (opened): Lelio Ribeiro De Paula, with FermatSearch, reports the factor 1,995,420,873 x 2^(7,222)+1 of F_7,220, dated 8 December 2024; total 371. The converted page text prints the exponent as '27,222', which reads as 2 followed by a flattened superscript 7,222, consistent with the printed index F_7,220 under the form k x 2^(m+2)+1. This reading is my inference from the flattened text.
events.delivers: F_7220 has a proper factor, so it is composite. One more explicit index. Does not move the universal claim beyond this index.
events.remains: The universal claim for all n > 4, and every other index.
events.directly_checkable: Test 2^(2^7220) = -1 mod 1995420873 x 2^7222+1: 7,220 modular squarings modulo a roughly 2,200-digit number. Cheap. Not run (see incomplete).
events.doubts: The index and exponent are read from flattened text (the converter dropped superscripts). The consistent reading is the one I give; the divisibility test would settle it.
events.object: Explicit proper factor 1,995,420,873 x 2^(7,222)+1 of F_7,220, as read from the page.

events.what_happened: FermatSearch news (opened): Serge Batalov and Ryan Propper, with FermatSearch, report the factor 39,701 x 2^414,679+1 of F_414,677, dated 10 January 2025; total 372.
events.delivers: F_414677 has a proper factor, so it is composite. One more explicit index.
events.remains: The universal claim for all n > 4, and every other index.
events.directly_checkable: 2^(2^414677) = -1 mod p for p of about 414,000 bits: about 414,000 modular squarings at that size. Heavy; not run.
events.object: Explicit proper factor 39,701 x 2^414,679+1 of F_414,677, as printed.

events.what_happened: FermatSearch news (opened): Valter Cavecchia, with PrimeGrid, reports the factor 99 x 2^(5,798,449)+1 of F_5,798,447, dated 14 January 2025; total 373. The same index is given in search results.
events.delivers: F_5798447 has a proper factor, so it is composite. One more explicit index.
events.remains: The universal claim for all n > 4, and every other index.
events.directly_checkable: Modular test with about 5.8 million squarings at a 5.8-million-bit modulus. Heavy; not run.
events.object: Explicit proper factor 99 x 2^(5,798,449)+1 of F_5,798,447, as printed.

events.what_happened: FermatSearch news (opened): Gary Gostin reports the factor 36,812,439,837 x 2^(3,144)+1, dated 27 November 2025, and prints the index as F_3,135; total 374. The printed exponent and the printed index disagree under the form k x 2^(m+2)+1: the exponent 3,144 implies index 3,142.
events.delivers: A proper factor of one Fermat number, so that number is composite. Which index it belongs to is not settled by the page (3,135 or 3,142). Either way it is one more explicit index.
events.remains: The universal claim for all n > 4, and every other index.
events.directly_checkable: Test 2^(2^3135) and 2^(2^3142) mod 36812439837 x 2^3144+1 for equality with -1. Each is about 3,140 modular squarings at a 950-digit modulus. Cheap. Not run (see incomplete).
events.doubts: The index conflict above. The divisibility test would settle which index is meant.
events.direction: Toward composite, for one index (3,135 or 3,142 as printed).
events.object: Explicit proper factor 36,812,439,837 x 2^(3,144)+1 of a Fermat number, the index printed as F_3,135.

events.what_happened: FermatSearch news (opened): Sascha Beat Dinkel and PrimeGrid report the factor 1085 x 2^(3,943,263)+1 of F_3,943,261, dated 3 December 2025. The page says it is at position 1,067 on PrimePages, has 1,187,044 digits, and brings the total to 375 known Fermat factors. The search snippet reads the factor as '23,943,263+1 is a Factor of F3,943,261', which agrees on the index.
events.delivers: F_3943261 has a proper factor, so it is composite. One more explicit index. The largest factor reported in the window, but still one index.
events.remains: The universal claim for all n > 4, and every other index.
events.directly_checkable: 2^(2^3943261) = -1 mod p for a 3.9-million-bit modulus: about 3.9 million modular squarings of very large numbers. Not feasible here; not run.
events.doubts: The FermatSearch factors page (opened) gives 374 known factors with a last-update date of 31 Mar 2026, one below the 375 in this news entry. The count conflict is unresolved.
events.object: Explicit proper factor 1085 x 2^(3,943,263)+1 of F_3,943,261, with 1,187,044 digits, as printed.

events.what_happened: A Prime Pages curio (opened, t5k.org) lists a 54-digit prime (printed 11692...73313) as the smallest prime factor of 2^(2^14)+1 = F_14. It was submitted 16 January 2026 and last modified 28 January 2026, credited to 'Marcel'. The page gives no discovery date and does not say whether the prime is new.
events.delivers: A known factor of F_14 is recorded again. Probably not a new discovery: OEIS A046052 (opened; last updated 2010) gives F_14 one known factor with a 4880-digit cofactor, and 54 + 4880 is consistent with F_14's about 4933 digits. The identity is inferred, not confirmed. Even if new, it would be one more composite index.
events.remains: The universal claim for all n > 4, and every other index.
events.directly_checkable: Divisibility of F_14 by the printed prime: 2^(2^14) = -1 mod p, which is 14 squarings. Cheap, but the printed prime is truncated, so the full value is needed. Not run.
events.doubts: The factor's identity with OEIS's recorded factor is inferred. The curio gives no discovery date.
events.direction: Toward composite, for index 14 (probably not new).
events.object: A 54-digit prime factor of F_14, as printed in truncated form on the curio page.

events.what_happened: Nobuki Fujimoto, with 'Rei' (Rei-AIOS autonomous research substrate) and 'Claude (Anthropic, claude-opus-4-7)' listed as co-authors, posts 'Fermat Numbers F_5-F_11: Empirical v_2(omega_{F_n}(3)) Measurement + Lean 4 Axiom-Free F_9 Excess Witness' (Rei-AIOS Paper 176). A HackMD draft is dated 20 July 2026; the Zenodo record (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21694136) gives publication 30 July 2026, version v0.1. The paper measures how far the 2-adic valuation of the order of 3 modulo F_n exceeds Lucas's 1878 bound for n = 5 to 11, and gives a Lean 4 file for the factor 2424833 = 37 x 2^16+1 of F_9, which the paper attributes to Selfridge and Hurwitz (1963).
events.revisions: HackMD draft 2026-07-20 (opened); Zenodo v0.1 published 2026-07-30 (opened). No later version found. A dev.to mirror exists (search result only).
events.delivers: On the composite question, nothing. The measured excess and the Lean witness concern F_5 to F_11, which are all already known composite, and the F_9 factor is long known. It does not establish compositeness of any F_n with n > 4.

machine_checked.system: Lean 4 with Mathlib v4.27.0, as reported by the authors
machine_checked.note: The authors report zero sorry, zero native_decide, zero user axioms. The Lean repository is listed as private in a search summary of the record, so the claim could not be checked.

events.doubts: Self-published draft, with an author-run axiom audit ('Axiom audit (Rei env #print axioms, actually run 2026-07-20)'). The Lean code is not publicly checkable. No independent review was found. The paper proposes replacing the Selfridge-Hurwitz attribution of the F_9 factor with a Lean-internal proof, so the attribution is itself under revision. The reference list gives Lenstra's F_9 result as 1993 where the prior-art section gives 1990 (from the summarised text).
events.direction: Does not bear on the composite question. Its F_9 factor is a known composite index, and its measurements cover indices already known composite.
events.object: A Lean 4 witness that 2424833 = 37 x 2^16+1 divides F_9 (known factor), plus a per-index table of excess over Lucas's bound for n = 5 to 11 (0, 0, 0, 1, 5, 0, 0 as reported).

systems.name: Claude (Anthropic, claude-opus-4-7)
systems.what_it_did: Per the authors, 'chat-Claude' privately extended the F_5 to F_8 measurements and provided an independent check of v_2(ord_{2424833}(3)) = 16, and the authors credit that work to chat-Claude's independent computation. The authors also list chat-Claude as a co-architect and in the acknowledgements. The authors describe a 'syntactic resemblance' flagged by chat-Claude as 'marker-level analogy only'. A summary of the text says chat-Claude suggested replacing the Selfridge-Hurwitz attribution with a Lean-internal proof; that is a paraphrase from a summarising fetch, not a verbatim sentence.

systems.name: Rei (Rei-AIOS autonomous research substrate)
systems.what_it_did: Per the authors: the F_5 to F_11 independent Python measurement, enforcement of an evaluation symmetry principle, and the Lean 4 file FermatNineExcessWitness.lean, which the authors call Rei-internal. The source calls it an autonomous research substrate and a 'Rei stack'. It does not say it is a language model, so the source does not establish whether it is an AI system, a pipeline, or an agent harness. Treat as an internal research system, not a shipped model.
systems.basis_quote: Rei-AIOS autonomous research substrate: F_5-F_11 independent Python measurement;

events.what_happened: A. Mayeux, 'The set of primes is supernatural: a Lean formalization of the statement of the conjecture', arXiv:2608.08643, submitted 9 August 2026. It formalises in Lean 4 over Mathlib the statement of a conjecture that no non-constant function built from the identity and constants, by finitely many additions, multiplications and exponentiations, sends every positive integer to a prime, and lists similar statements as open problems.
events.delivers: Nothing on Fermat numbers. The abstract page opened does not mention Fermat numbers; a search summary said the paper uses Euler's F_5 factorisation as an example, which I could not confirm on the page.

machine_checked.note: Sorry-free per the abstract as summarised; not independently checked.

events.direction: Not applicable: a formalisation of a different conjecture.

events.what_happened: Jiri Klaska, 'Several Notes on Jakobczyk's Hypothesis on Fermat Numbers', Integers 26 (2026), article A77. Its introduction restates Jakobczyk's 1951 hypothesis that every Fermat number is square-free, calls it unresolved, and places it among generalised Fermat sequences. The PDF could not be decoded; only the introduction, as summarised in search results, was read.
events.delivers: Not about compositeness. It concerns square-freeness, a separate Wikipedia bullet. From the excerpt, no composite-index result is reported.

checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted for publication. Per search summary: received April 2025, revised July 2026, published June 2026. Not verified on the page.

events.what_happened: Peter Chocian, 'The Primitive Generalized Fermat Equation x^3+y^5=z^7: A computer-assisted proof', arXiv:2609.26996, submitted 22 September 2026. The abstract claims no solutions in nonzero coprime integers, building on Dahmen-Siksek and Putz and excluding seven septic fields, with finite calculations supplied as certificates. The page's comments field says 'Substantial AI-assisted research and writing; see the statement in Section 8'. Section 8 was not read.
events.delivers: Nothing on Fermat numbers 2^(2^n)+1. It concerns a generalised Fermat equation.

summary: Sources used: Wikipedia's Fermat number article (Dec 2025 snapshot) and Wikipedia's List of unsolved problems in mathematics, which carries the bullet 'Is every Fermat number 2^(2^n)+1 composite for n > 4?'; the FermatSearch news and factors pages; OEIS A046052; a Prime Pages curio; arXiv abstracts; the Rei-AIOS note on HackMD and Zenodo. The problem as stated is a single universal claim. The known state: F_0 to F_4 are prime, and no Fermat prime beyond F_4 is known. Compositeness is known for 5 <= n <= 32 (Wikipedia, Dec 2025), with F_20 and F_24 having no known factor (F_24 has a non-constructive proof, 2001/2003). Since 26 January 2024, the events bearing on the question are seven explicit prime factors of individual Fermat numbers: F_251 (24 May 2024), F_223380 (4 Jul 2024), F_7220 (8 Dec 2024), F_414677 (10 Jan 2025), F_5798447 (14 Jan 2025), an index for the 27 Nov 2025 factor that the page gives as 3,135 but whose exponent implies 3,142, and F_3943261 (3 Dec 2025). Each adds one composite index. Under DEEP_DIVE 2.1 each is one instance of a universal claim and moves nothing, so each is recorded as an event that does not move the bullet. No 2026 factor was found in the sources read (the FermatSearch news ends at 3 Dec 2025). The Dec 2025 total is inconsistent between the news page (375) and the factors page (374, last updated 31 Mar 2026). The 2026 PrimePages curio on F_14 is probably an old factor. No mathematician has publicly checked any of the factors beyond the announcing sites, and the factor itself is the check. AI: no AI system is credited with any of the factor finds, which were run with gfs and PrimeGrid software on personal hardware per the FermatSearch page. The one event that names AI systems is the Rei-AIOS note (HackMD draft 20 Jul 2026, Zenodo v0.1 30 Jul 2026), which credits 'Claude (Anthropic, claude-opus-4-7)' as co-architect and 'chat-Claude' with measurements and a check, and the Rei research substrate with Python measurement and a Lean file. Its subject is the Lucas-bound excess of F_5 to F_11 and a Lean witness of the long-known F_9 factor 2424833. It does not bear on compositeness for n > 4, and it is self-published with an unchecked Lean repository. Name collisions I checked and set aside: Anthropic's September 2026 formalisation of Fermat's Last Theorem (not opened; search snippet only, not about Fermat numbers); arXiv 2609.26996 (opened; it is about x^3+y^5=z^7 and does not name the tools a search snippet attributed to it; its comment says only 'Substantial AI-assisted research and writing'). Searches for OpenAI, Gemini/DeepMind, AlphaEvolve/FunSearch and Anthropic credit on Fermat-number factors found nothing. Close calls: whether the factor finds should count as events at all (they are recorded and move nothing under 2.1); the F_3,135/3,142 index conflict (unresolved, the divisibility check was not run); the first-written date for the F_24 paper (1999 computation, 2001 preprint per a summary, 2003 journal).
competing_reading: Counting proven composite indices, seven new explicit factors since May 2024 (and the index-3,943,261 factor in particular) look like steady progress on 'is F_n composite for n > 4', and a reader could record each as a case settled. Under the scope rule each is one more instance of a universal claim, so none moves the bullet. For the AI question, a reader could count the Rei-AIOS note's Claude co-authorship as load-bearing for that paper, which it may well be for its own claims, while noting that the paper does not bear on this bullet. Heuristic evidence (Boklan and Conway 2016; Wikipedia's 'F_4 is the last Fermat prime' remark) points toward the composite answer, but it is not a proof.
what_would_settle_it: For the universal claim: either a general argument producing a proper factor or a compositeness proof for every F_n with n > 4, or a prime F_n with n > 4 (a deterministic Pepin test would confirm primality). For this record: a divisibility test of the 27 Nov 2025 factor at indices 3,135 and 3,142 (pow(2, 2^m, p) == p-1), the small in-window factors (F_251 and F_7220), the current FermatSearch count (374 or 375), the authors' verbatim AI sentences in the Rei-AIOS note beyond the quotes captured here, and the full text of the Integers 2026 paper if it mentions compositeness.

judgement.why: The statement is a single universal claim over all n > 4. Every factor find, before and after the snapshot, and the F_24 Pepin proof, settles one index, so each is a finite instance of the universal claim (F5) and is scored instances. That includes Euler's F_5, which is a counterexample to Fermat's original belief but confirms this statement at one index only. The Boklan-Conway heuristic proves nothing, so it is none. Detto, Mayeux, Klaska (square-freeness) and Chocian answer different questions, so they are variant. Klaska's year-only 2026 date still falls clearly after January 2024. The Rei-AIOS note does not bear on the problem (none). For its own AI role, Claude's extended measurements are computed content in that paper, so I scored it assisted. That was a close call against none, and it does not matter here because the event is discarded. Chocian has an AI disclosure but no recorded systems, so it is none.
judgement.doubts: Rei's 'autonomous research substrate' is not established to be an AI model and is not credited. The F_3,135/3,142 index conflict and the 374/375 count conflict are unresolved but immaterial to the scope.
